* NBA legend Charles Barkley begins 3-day jail sentence for DUI conviction
* TNT analyst is serving time in Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio's "Tent City"
* Barkley on his sentence: "I screwed up ... I've got to pay the piper"
* Sheriff Arpaio says Barkley will wear striped jumpsuit, get "no special treatment"

***

**PHOENIX, Arizona (CNN)** -- Decked out in jail-issued black-and-white stripes rather than his usual custom suit, NBA Hall of Famer Charles Barkley began serving his three-day DUI sentence Saturday at Maricopa County's infamous "Tent City" jail, promising to take his punishment "like a man."

Barkley, 46, checked into the facility shortly after sunrise following a December arrest in nearby Scottsdale, Arizona, where police stopped him after he ran a stop sign. Tests later revealed his blood-alcohol level was nearly twice the legal limit.

"I made a mistake. I screwed up, and I'm paying the price," Barkley told reporters outside the tent enclosure before being processed. "I’m not going to sit here and whine about it. I’m a big boy. I’m 46 years old, and I’ve got to take responsibility for my actions."

**'America's Toughest Sheriff' meets 'The Round Mound of Rebound'**

The short sentence brings together two of Phoenix’s most outspoken public figures: Barkley, the candid TNT *Inside the NBA* studio analyst, and Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, the self-proclaimed "Toughest Sheriff in America."

Arpaio, famous for forcing inmates to wear pink underwear, sleep in unconditioned military tents, and work on chain gangs, held a press conference alongside Barkley prior to the basketball star’s booking.

Despite Arpaio's hardline reputation, the dynamic between the conservative sheriff and the politically unpredictable basketball star was surprisingly warm, punctuated by moments of lighthearted banter.

"He's being treated like every other inmate," Arpaio told CNN. "He gets the striped uniform, he gets the pink underwear, and he gets the two meals a day—which are mostly bologna. No television, no special privileges."

However, Arpaio conceded that for safety reasons, Barkley is being housed in an isolated, tented enclosure separate from the general inmate population. 

"I have a responsibility to keep him safe," Arpaio said. "He’s a high-profile guy. But make no mistake, he’s sleeping on a cot in a tent."

Barkley joked about his upcoming accommodations, telling reporters he planned to use the downtime to catch up on sleep and perhaps shed a few pounds.

"The sheriff told me the food is terrible, so maybe I'll lose five or ten pounds in here," Barkley quipped. "I brought a couple of books, and I'm just going to sit back, reflect on my life, and make sure I never put myself or anyone else in this position again."

**Earning respect from the Sheriff**

While Arpaio is known for using celebrity arrests to highlight his tough-on-crime policies, he praised Barkley for his attitude throughout the legal process.

"A lot of celebrities try to get out of it, or they complain and make excuses," Arpaio said. "Charles didn't do that. He stood up, admitted he was wrong, and accepted his sentence without crying about it. I respect that."

Arpaio revealed that Barkley had offered to record public service announcements warning young people about the dangers of drunk driving once his sentence is complete. 

Barkley, who spent eight seasons playing for the Phoenix Suns in the 1990s and still maintains a residence in the area, admitted that his relationship with Arpaio had evolved over the ordeal.

"I’ve always respected Sheriff Joe, even if I didn’t agree with everything he did," Barkley said. "He's run a tough ship here, but he’s been a straight shooter with me. I respect a guy who tells it to you straight."

**Return to TNT planned**

Barkley was originally sentenced to 10 days in jail, but the judge suspended seven days after Barkley agreed to complete an alcohol treatment program and pay more than $2,000 in fines. 

Network executives at TNT, who briefly suspended Barkley following his arrest, confirmed that he is expected to return to the anchor desk for the network’s coverage of the upcoming NBA playoffs.

Before being led away by sheriff's deputies to exchange his street clothes for inmate stripes, Barkley offered a final piece of advice to his fans.

"Don't drive drunk, man. Period," Barkley said. "Call a cab. Call a friend. It isn’t worth it. I got lucky that nobody got hurt. That's the biggest lesson out of all of this."

Barkley is scheduled to be released early Tuesday morning.
